11:1.sourceText: Καὶ ὅτε ἐγγίζουσιν εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα εἰς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν πρὸς τὸ ὄρος τῶν Ἐλαιῶν, ἀποστέλλει δύο τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ
11:1.targetText: And when they come near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage, and Bethany, to the Mount of Olives, He sends forth two of His disciples,

11:2.sourceText: καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς Ὑπάγετε εἰς τὴν κώμην τὴν κατέναντι ὑμῶν, καὶ εὐθὺς εἰσπορευόμενοι εἰς αὐτὴν εὑρήσετε πῶλον δεδεμένον ἐφ’ ὃν οὐδεὶς οὔπω ἀνθρώπων ἐκάθισεν· λύσατε αὐτὸν καὶ φέρετε.
11:2.targetText: and says to them, “Go away into the village that is in front of you, and immediately, entering into it, you will find a colt tied, on which no one of men has sat, having loosed it, bring [it]:

groups.note: N1904 uses an imperative loose; LSV uses having loosed in the coordinated instruction. The actual loosening head remains anchored with the mood/construction difference explicit.
The written colt object αὐτόν is shared by loosing and bringing; English repeats the same object as bracketed it with bring.

unmappedSource.reason: N1904 οὔπω adds not yet to the no-one-has-sat clause; LSV/TR expresses no one has sat without a separate yet component.
Greek explicitly joins loose and bring with καί; LSV uses having loosed before bring without a separate connective.

unmappedTarget.reason: English supplies the copula in the village that is in front; Greek has an article-plus-prepositional modifier without a be verb.

11:3.sourceText: καὶ ἐάν τις ὑμῖν εἴπῃ Τί ποιεῖτε τοῦτο; εἴπατε Ὁ Κύριος αὐτοῦ χρείαν ἔχει, καὶ εὐθὺς αὐτὸν ἀποστέλλει πάλιν ὧδε.
11:3.targetText: and if anyone may say to you, Why do you do this? Say that the LORD has need of it, and immediately He will send it here.”

groups.note: N1904 has present sends in the assurance; LSV uses future will send. The sending head remains anchored, without manufacturing a Greek future form.

unmappedSource.reason: N1904 πάλιν says again/back with sending it here; LSV/TR has no separately expressed back adverb.

unmappedTarget.reason: English supplies that to introduce the reported saying; Greek directly gives the Lord clause without a that conjunction.

11:4.sourceText: καὶ ἀπῆλθον καὶ εὗρον πῶλον δεδεμένον πρὸς θύραν ἔξω ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀμφόδου, καὶ λύουσιν αὐτόν.
11:4.targetText: And they went away, and found the colt tied at the door outside, by the two ways, and they loose it,

groups.note: The street/round-street noun ἄμφοδον is interpreted by LSV as the meeting of two ways. This complete locative phrase records that contextual translation, without inventing a separate Greek two numeral or two way nouns.

11:5.sourceText: καί τινες τῶν ἐκεῖ ἑστηκότων ἔλεγον αὐτοῖς Τί ποιεῖτε λύοντες τὸν πῶλον;
11:5.targetText: and certain of those standing there said to them, “What do you—loosing the colt?”

11:6.sourceText: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν αὐτοῖς καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· καὶ ἀφῆκαν αὐτούς.
11:6.targetText: And they said to them as Jesus commanded, and they permitted them.

groups.note: N1904 uses said, εἶπεν, for Jesus’ prior instruction; LSV commanded identifies the directive speech act in that context, without claiming that every saying verb means command.

11:11.sourceText: Καὶ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα εἰς τὸ ἱερόν· καὶ περιβλεψάμενος πάντα, ὀψὲ ἤδη οὔσης τῆς ὥρας, ἐξῆλθεν εἰς Βηθανίαν μετὰ τῶν δώδεκα.

groups.note: Greek describes the hour as late, ὀψὲ ... τῆς ὥρας; LSV compresses that late-hour circumstance to evening. The actual hour and lateness constituent jointly support that time description, not an isolated hour=evening equation.
